newsitem.title: USA: Year 2000 stocks plunge as Soros speculation quashed.
newsitem.headline: Year 2000 stocks plunge as Soros speculation quashed.

text.p: Shares of Zitel Corp. tumbled 33 percent Monday after speculation was squelched that the closely watched investor George Soros was interested in buying a stake in the computer software and services company.

Zitel's decline pushed down the stocks of other companies that specialize in fixing the so-called Year 2000 Bug, a software glitch in many computers making them unable to accurately recognize dates including the year 2000 or beyond.
Shares of Zitel, based in Fremont, Calif., fell $20.25 to $41 as 11.2 million shares traded on Nasdaq. It was the most actively traded stock in the United States Monday.

The stock had tripled in the past three weeks because of Zitel's stake in MatriDigm Corp., a software company that is working on automating the task of rewriting computer programs that may crash as of Jan. 1, 2000.

"Zitel has assumed the role of the poster child of the Year 2000," said Joe Besecker, analyst at money management firm Emerald Research. Its stock has swung wildly as investors' appetite for Year 2000 issues has fluctuated, he said.
In the past month, the stock also had risen on speculation that Soros, whose investment strategy is copied by other fund managers, was interested in buying a stake in Zitel.

A spokesman at Soros Fund Management has declined repeatedly to say whether Soros owns or is interested in buying shares of Zitel. But a person close to the fund said Monday that Soros did not own a stake in Zitel and was not planning to buy one.
That sent many investors heading for the exits, not only in Zitel but other Year 2000 issues.
Accelr8 Technology Corp. slipped $5.125 to $16.375. Data Dimensions Corp. fell $4.125 to $33.625. And TSR Inc. dived $7.50 to $30.
The stocks are extremely volatile because there are few places for investors to place their bets on the Year 2000 issue, said Jim Duggan, an analyst at First Albany Corp.

While the demand for Year 2000 fixes is huge -- by one estimate as much as $600 billion -- many of the companies in the field are tiny, Duggan said. Many will not have the resources to pursue contracts.
Meanwhile, as the end of the century looms closer, investors are weighing the merits of each company's products.
Setting aside the potential for wild swings, Zitel's MetriDigm is the best bet, Besecker said.
"To me, it doesn't matter if George Soros, Warren Buffett or Peter Lynch invest in it," Besecker said. "What matters is the technology."
The episode had the whiff of market mania, analysts said.

"This was like the biotech craze of 1991, only faster," said Scott Bleier, chief investment strategist at Prime Charter Ltd. "There may still be some interest in these stocks later, but this was a bubble that got way out of control."
